title: Exception Handling in PL/pgSQL
description: Handle runtime database errors, catch specific SQLSTATE codes, and raise custom exceptions.

data.text: In PL/pgSQL functions and stored procedures, exceptions can be caught and handled using `BEGIN ... EXCEPTION WHEN ... THEN` blocks.

data.title: Catching Unique Constraint Violations in PL/pgSQL

data.text: Catch the most specific condition first, because `WHEN others` swallows everything and hides bugs. Inside the handler, `SQLSTATE` holds the five-character code and `SQLERRM` holds the message. Use `RAISE` to re-raise when the error is not something you can meaningfully handle.

data.title: Specific handling, then custom errors
data.content: The handler retries on a foreign key violation and raises a domain-specific error otherwise.

data.title: Interview angle: exception blocks are subtransactions
data.text: Entering a `BEGIN ... EXCEPTION` block creates an implicit savepoint, and catching an error rolls back to it. That means all changes made inside the protected block before the error are discarded, not just the failed statement. The performance cost is a savepoint per block, so putting an exception block inside a tight loop is expensive. Knowing that an exception handler is a subtransaction explains both the semantics and the overhead.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Use `EXCEPTION WHEN condition` to catch runtime errors.
`SQLSTATE` and `SQLERRM` provide error codes and descriptive text.
Exception blocks create internal subtransactions with minor performance overhead.
